module: Mark synthetic outputs and verify detection

lesson.title: Editing assistance and the marking exceptions
lesson.summary: Apply the editing and authorised-law-enforcement exceptions without blanket claims.

prerequisites.reason: The learner must establish whether the Act reaches the scenario.
The learner must recognise generated or manipulated output and its modality. The learner must distinguish machine marking from human-facing labels.

blocks: The marking duty does not apply to the extent a system performs an **assistive function for standard editing**, or does not substantially alter provided input data or its semantics. Semantics means meaning.
These are alternatives in the provision. Record the actual function and degree of alteration; 'has an editing button' does not exempt every output from a wider generation system.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 50(2), sentence 3; Guidelines paragraphs 89-93
Commission Article 50 Guidelines C(2026) 5054 final; non-binding interpretation

blocks: A routine correction that leaves supplied content and meaning substantially unchanged differs from generating new arguments or materially replacing a scene. The Commission gives examples to help distinguish the cases.

Harbour compares correction of a spelling error with rewriting a statement to assert the opposite conclusion. The second is a substantive semantic change; it cannot claim the no-substantial-alteration alternative on these facts.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 50(2), sentence 3; Guidelines paragraphs 89-93
Commission Article 50 Guidelines C(2026) 5054 final; non-binding interpretation

blocks: Apply the exception **to the extent** the qualifying function is performed. A mixed product may offer standard assistance and substantive content generation.

Do not turn uncertainty about one output into a system-wide exemption. Keep evidence of what the feature actually changes. Technical feasibility affects the separate quality assessment; it is not this editing test.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 50(2), sentence 3; Guidelines paragraphs 89-93
Commission Article 50 Guidelines C(2026) 5054 final; non-binding interpretation

blocks: There is a distinct exception where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Merely intending to investigate wrongdoing is insufficient to establish legal authorisation.

In a stipulated case with that authorisation, use the exact paragraph 2 exception. Do not copy its wording to every other paragraph: the conditions differ. Other applicable duties and law still need analysis.

questions.prompt: An AI feature corrects a spelling error without substantially changing the supplied content or meaning. Which exception should Harbour examine?

options.reason: Those alternatives concern qualifying assistance and alteration.

options.blocks: A universal exception for all AI-written text
options.reason: The provision does not exempt all generated text.

options.blocks: An exemption based only on the feature's name
options.reason: Actual function and output changes matter.

questions.prompt: One feature corrects spelling; another generates a new claim contradicting the input. Can Harbour exempt both solely because the product is an editor?

options.blocks: Yes; an editing interface exempts the whole system
options.reason: That ignores 'to the extent' and substantial changes.
The semantics of the input are expressly relevant.

options.blocks: No; apply the exception to qualifying functions and outputs
options.reason: The scope is limited by what the system actually performs or alters.
